title: No extension of the Quantum Tensor Product admits a Superposition principle
abstract: Textbook quantum superposition refers to the feature that certain linear combinations of Hilbert space rays, each representing a valid quantum state, are themselves valid states. This notion is not operational, and it relies on the underlying Hilbert space formalism. Recent proposals for experimental tests of indefinite causal order, as well as tests probing the non-classicality of gravity, pivot on superposition, thereby calling for a theory-independent, operational formalisation of the concept. Here, we define superposition within the framework of Generalised Probabilistic Theories, based on observed statistics in prepare-and-measure experiments. Using this, we formulate three superposition principles to investigate which structural features of quantum theory carry over to other theories. We study conditions under which these principles carry over from subsystems to their compositions; to this end, we show that the quantum tensor product emerges as the largest composition rule for quantum systems respecting all three principles. Furthermore, we show how non-classical features such as entanglement and preparational uncertainty can be viewed as special forms of superposition.
summary: This paper redefines quantum superposition operationally within Generalized Probabilistic Theories (GPTs), removing reliance on Hilbert space formalism. By testing three structural superposition principles, the authors demonstrate that the quantum tensor product is the largest composition rule consistent with these principles. This work provides deep insights into the necessary structural axioms underlying quantum theory.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop a theory-independent, operational definition of quantum superposition, moving beyond the reliance on the Hilbert space formalism, and to determine which structural features of quantum theory are necessary for this concept.
main_result: The quantum tensor product emerges as the largest composition rule for quantum systems that respects all three formulated superposition principles. Furthermore, the authors show that no extension of the quantum tensor product admits a universal superposition principle.
method: The authors define superposition operationally within the framework of Generalised Probabilistic Theories (GPTs) using prepare-and-measure statistics, and test this definition using three structural superposition principles (complete, uniform, and mutual).
model_or_system: The analysis uses Generalised Probabilistic Theories (GPTs) to model various physical systems, including quantum theory, classical theory, and abstract 'g-systems.' Composite systems are analyzed using tensor product structures for state and effect spaces.
key_observables: Superposition itself (defined relationally in GPTs), preparational uncertainty, and entanglement are shown to be special forms of superposition.
important_parameters: The structure of the underlying GPT, the set of extremal states (MPD set), and the specific superposition principles (Complete, Uniform, Mutual).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the set of MDE measurements is informationally complete for the system under study.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the operational definition of superposition in GPTs, then formulates and tests the three superposition principles (Complete, Uniform, Mutual) across various GPTs. It then analyzes the composition rules for these principles, culminating in the proof that the quantum tensor product is the maximal structure satisfying these principles.
why_interesting: This work provides a fundamental, axiomatic investigation into the core concept of superposition, which is crucial for understanding the boundaries between quantum mechanics and other physical theories, impacting foundational quantum information theory.

FIG. 3. State space of the regular pentagon (n = 5). The MPD set {ω5(1), ω5(4)} is highlighted; vertices lying on the blue dotted lines correspond to the deterministic extremal states of either the MDEs M1 = {e5(1), u −e5(1)} or M4 = {e5(4), u −e5(4)}. For each vertex not belonging to the MPD set, we indicate the MDE(s) for which they are probabilistic. Those that are probabilistic with respect to a single MDE are the extremal states that, while in a superposition of {ω5(1), ω5(4)}, form an MPD set with one of its elements.
